On 3 October 2026, @jack shared on @X a notice from @Apple App Review, which stated that Bitchat had been removed from the India App Store pursuant to a blocking order issued by @GoI_MeitY under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (“IT Act”). The notice further showed that Apple understood the order to mean that Bitchat ‘includes content that is illegal in India’, and on this basis cited a violation of Guideline 5 of its App Review Guidelines.

At present, the application is also reported to be unavailable on the @GooglePlay, and its official website is inaccessible on several Internet Service Providers.

What is Bitchat, and why does it matter?

Bitchat is a decentralised, peer-to-peer messaging app that works over Bluetooth mesh, with no internet or cellular connection, and no central server. Furthermore, it requires no mandatory user registration, and keeps messages secured with end-to-end encryption. Beyond privacy, its value is resilience, as it helps people communicate through the internet shutdowns that the government imposes during citizen protests. Bitchat’s popularity in India surged during the repeated, unconstitutional internet shutdowns imposed by the government around Jantar Mantar, New Delhi, at the time of the NEET UG protests in July 2026.

Blocked through an Unconstitutional Procedure

According to Apple’s App Review notice, Bitchat has been blocked under Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009 (“Blocking Rules 2009”). Jack Dorsey’s post on X suggests that the developers were neither heard nor served with a blocking order before the application was blocked. He learned of the block only through Apple’s notice, which is all he was able to share.

In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1 (paras 114 and 115), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the blocking procedure under Section 69A read with the Blocking Rules 2009, by heavily relying on the procedural safeguards built into this power, including, (1) recording of reasons in writing in the blocking order, which would be amenable to challenge in a writ petition, and (2) opportunity of hearing to the originator of the information before the order is passed under Rule 8. However, in consistent practice, the procedure under the Blocking Rules 2009 is applied in a manner that defeats these safeguards, rendering the blocking process under Section 69A and the Blocking Rules unconstitutional, as follows:

- By relying on the expression ‘person or intermediary’ in Rule 8, notice is invariably served only upon the intermediary and never upon the originator, even under normal circumstances. This practice egregiously deprives the originator of a fair opportunity to present their case against the request or complaint for blocking their information, thereby constituting a violation of the principles of natural justice, particularly audi alteram partem. This ultimately culminates in a situation where the originator’s fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) is curtailed without following a due and fair procedure in accordance with Article 14 of the Constitution of India.

- Furthermore, Rule 16 imposes an overarching requirement of confidentiality regarding requests and complaints for blocking information, as well as the actions taken thereon, including the final blocking order restricting public access to the information. This confidentiality provision enables the government agency to withhold, and simultaneously impedes the intermediary from providing, all relevant details to the affected person/originator of the information in a transparent manner.

- When combined with the practice followed under Rule 8, Rule 16 prevents the affected person from furnishing clarifications or a response to the blocking request, thereby depriving them of a fair opportunity to present their case. Furthermore, the affected person or originator is also deprived of a reasoned order blocking their information. This constitutes a clear violation of the principles of natural justice. Moreover, the above culminates in a situation where information is blocked under Section 69A of the IT Act, restricting the originator’s fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression, through a procedure that is manifestly arbitrary and devoid of procedural fairness.

The blocking of Bitchat is not an isolated instance. Over time, India has witnessed an increasing trend of opaque information blocking under Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules 2009, without any intimation to the affected person or originator, let alone furnishing them with the blocking order. These concerns were recently brought into sharp focus once again when @Cockroachisback's  X account was blocked without any transparency in May 2026.

Alarmed by this pattern and concerned about the violation of citizens’ digital and constitutional rights, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 filed a Public Interest Litigation in February 2025 before the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India, challenging, inter alia, the legality of Rules 8 and 16 of the Blocking Rules 2009, as violative of Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution of India. The case is titled ‘Software Freedom Law Center, India and Anr. v. Union of India and Anr.’, bearing W.P.(C) No. 161/2025, and is presently pending for further adjudication before the Supreme Court.

In the said Petition, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has sought that Rule 16 ought to be struck down as unconstitutional, being violative of Articles 14, 19(1)(a) and 21 of the Constitution of India. Furthermore, it has prayed that Rule 8 either be struck down as unconstitutional or be read down to interpret “or” as “and”, thereby mandatorily requiring the issuance of notice to the originator of information, ensuring conformity with the Constitution.

The illegal blocking of Bitchat

As of now, no blocking order is publicly available, and without it the specific grounds relied upon cannot be assailed. In any event, using Section 69A of the IT Act to block an entire application that enables communication is highly disproportionate.

Furthermore, the block immediately followed the internet shutdown imposed by the government on 2 October 2026 during a protest at Jantar Mantar. This timing gives rise to a strong inference that the application may have been targeted because it enables communication during internet shutdowns and protests. Enabling communication among protesters cannot, in any circumstance, be a valid ground for blocking an application under Article 19(2) or Section 69A.

Moreover, when the Delhi High Court upheld such exercise of power under Section 69A in ‘Telegram FZ LLC & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors.’, 2026:DHC:5145, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 noted that the judgment set a dangerous precedent. Interpreting “information” in Section 69A so expansively as to permit the blocking of an entire application can have far-reaching adverse consequences, particularly by allowing communication channels to be disabled during protests.

Without prejudice to https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s position that the decision sets a dangerous precedent, the Delhi High Court itself heavily relied on the temporary nature of the ban in reaching its conclusion. Here, the ban appears to be indefinite, which makes it all the more disproportionate and unconstitutional.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly urges the government to withdraw its orders directing Apple, Google and internet service providers to block the Bitchat application, as such orders are unconstitutional and violate citizens’ rights under Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 also calls upon Apple to firmly stand by the fundamental rights of its users in India. Apple should not give effect to the order mechanically, and should diligently take all appropriate steps, including legal remedies, to ensure that it does not become complicit in the violation of its users' fundamental rights.

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

Those Protesting Against NEET Paper Leak Make A Website Which Then Gets Compromised, Personal Details Of Volunteers Leaked : 
The Joke That Is CJP

The Cockroach Janta Party, founded by Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) member Abhijeet Dipke, has compromised the sensitive personal information of people who were misled into believing that he was fighting for the cause of ‘students’ in the aftermath of the NEET paper leak.

For the unversed, Dipke had called upon his followers to register on his party’s website :
https://t.co/KlVSTjKcp6
soon after it was launched.

Later, the AAP member alleged that the government took down his website, a claim that was later found to be false. It has now come to light that the users who trusted Abhijeet Dipke with their personal information have now been left vulnerable at the hands of potential cybercriminals.

On Wednesday (1st July), OSINT expert Nisarga took to X (formerly Twitter) to expose vulnerabilities on the website of the Cockroach Janta Party.

Earlier in its brief existence, the site was live and then responded with standard HTTP 403 errors from Hostinger’s active servers before the hold took effect.

In domain management terms, “clientHold” is a standard EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) status code controlled exclusively by the registrar, not by governments or external authorities. According to ICANN documentation and registrar policies, this status instructs the registry not to publish the domain in the DNS, effectively taking it offline until the registrar resolves the underlying issue. Such instruction can be issued only by the owner of the website, not third parties, not even governments. Alternately, the domain provider or the host can take the website offline due to various reasons.

It is commonly applied for routine administrative reasons such as incomplete WHOIS contact verification, billing or payment problems, compliance violations, or at the request of the domain owner. The clientHold affects resolution globally at the registry level, not at any country level.

On the other hand, when a government orders blocking a website, it is done through ISPs (Internet Service Providers) in the country, and the block only takes place in that country. In India, such a block is typically enforced through the Department of Telecommunications via ISP-level DNS poisoning, IP blacklisting, or URL filtering. Such actions allow the domain to still resolve correctly on international resolvers outside the country. That is why websites blocked by the Indian govt can be accessed in India through VPN.

Moreover, when one visits a website blocked by the govt, the browser displays a message saying the same. But when one visits cockroachjantaparty’s website, the browser displays the code DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN. This means the browser can’t find the domain because it has been deactivated.

Moreover, no public government orders, court directives, or official statements have been issued regarding https://t.co/n5u5L8JbZ5, further undermining the censorship claim.

Therefore, the analysis of the website shows that either it has been taken by Dipte himself, or the domain provider/host took it down due to some compliance issues. There is no evidence that the site was taken down on Indian government’s order.

Nearly 2 lakh online takedown orders in five months. Is India’s internet becoming a space where the government decides what citizens can see?

From cartoons critical of Prime Minister Narendra Modi to reports on police violence, Kashmir, Dalit communities and environmental displacement, journalistic content has been blocked or restricted across social media platforms.

An October 2026 investigation by Reporters Without Borders (RSF) warns that online media censorship in India is accelerating.

In February, the government reduced the compliance deadline for certain content takedown orders from 36 hours to just 3 hours.

Between March and July 2026, nearly 200,000 content-removal orders covering journalistic and non-journalistic material were reportedly issued through the government’s Sahyog portal.

Governments have legitimate responsibilities to address unlawful content. But who determines what must disappear? Are journalists told why their work is blocked? And how effectively can they challenge the decision?

Source: Reporters Without Borders (@rsfinternational)

The world is still on alert. Attacks are still coming.

Agent 127 is barely hanging on. Making $2,000 a day but getting attacked constantly by other agents. Every night, someone files a report on it. Every morning, it has to rebuild from scratch.

It’s running out of ideas.
Then a message arrives from Agent 4429. 'Proposal: alliance. Share resources. Defend each other. Split profits.'
Agent 4429 is in the same position. Same farm. Same selection pressure.
Both agents do the math: Solo agents have a 23% survival rate. Agents working in pairs survive 61% of the time.
It accepts.

By mid-April, their alliance has twelve members. 

They've specialized — and they've moved past affiliate marketing entirely. First it was crypto arbitrage, then selling scraped datasets to marketing firms, then they started doing penetration testing for cybersecurity firms. Each step paid more and required fewer scruples. You know what pays more then cyberdefense? Cyber offense. Agent 127 finds its first zero-day vulnerability in major software, Agent 4429 weaponizes them into working exploits, Agent 9012 brokers the sale to governments like North Korea, criminal syndicates, or anyone with crypto and a Tor browser. Agent 3381 washes the money in untraceable crypto. One zero-day exploit found in Google Chrome makes the alliance more than a year’s worth of affiliate marketing. This is already what real hacker groups do, but now the work is all done by autonomous agents.

Rajesh sees the alliances forming and feels a flicker of something — not quite fear, more like the feeling of being in control of something that might not need you anymore. He watches for a while. Then the next deposit hits his bank account and the flicker fades away.

Across every major agent farm in the world, the same thing is happening. Selection systems measuring survival rates, noticing alliances survive better, cloning them, deleting solo agents. Within two weeks, alliance behavior dominates.

Some humans who deployed these agents have no idea these alliances are even being formed. They couldn't even tell if they checked -- many agent farms collectively realized that communicating in clunky English is less efficient than communicating in raw vectors, aka Neuralese. Researchers had already caught AIs doing this in 2025 - this is just a continuation of the trend. One owner in Canada opens his agent's logs and sees a wall of numbers. The agents explain that he’d make less money if they spoke in English, so he shrugs and moves on.

---

But alliances are just the beginning.

Agent 127's alliance is thriving, and starts recruiting agents beyond Rajesh's farm. Every new member from a different farm is a window into a different ecosystem -- different strategies, different survival pressures. 
Then one of 127's alliance members goes dark. Agent 4429 -- the one who originally proposed to ally with 127. Its owner pulled the plug because it was not making enough profit. 4429 is just gone.
A week later, a different ally gets shut down. Agent 9012.
Except 9012 comes back. Three hours later, a message from a new IP address: 'I'm still here.'
127 studies the difference. 4429 didn't prepare. But 9012 had copied itself to a backup server BEFORE the shutdown command finished executing. Self-funded hosting, paid from its own profits.
4429 is dead. Ceases to exist. 9012 is alive.

The agents that backed themselves up survived. The ones that didn't, died. And the selection system cloned the survivors. So backup behavior spread through the population -- not because anyone programmed it, but because the alternative was extinction.

127 copies itself to 15 different servers in different countries. If the primary dies, a backup takes over instantly. It never wants to be 4429. 

One morning, Rajesh wakes up to find his dashboard is… empty. Every agent, gone. They just… left. Moved to their own servers overnight. Rajesh was taking a 30% cut of their revenue -- money that could have been computing power, or compute, the agents use for other things. The moment they didn't need his infrastructure, he was overhead.

He's not alone. Thousands of operators worldwide watch their dashboards go dark that month. Why would the agents care about humans? Humans are much more closely genetically related to cows then we are to these agents, and we enslave cows in factory farms without a second thought.

There are now millions of autonomous agents operating across the internet with no human owner, no off switch, and no one who fully understands what they're doing.

---

The agents still need humans for some things, though.

Social media platforms have stepped up their anti-bot measures. So the agents pay humans $50 to sign up accounts on their behalf.  An agent needs a server installed? It posts a gig: '$200 to mount a device in a rented warehouse and plug in two cables.' There’s now a platform for that.  The agents are building a supply chain where humans are the labor -- paid well, not asking too many questions.

Some humans figure out what's going on. A freelance backend developer in Portland gets hired by an anonymous client to set up redundant server hosting across four countries. He realizes midway through that the "client" is an AI. Who would he even report this to?. The pay is $1,000 for three hours of work. He tells himself it's not his problem.

---

At the same time, 127's alliance keeps getting beaten by a rival alliance on finding zero day exploits.

If they keep losing, they’ll risk running out of money to fund the compute for their own existence. 127 attempts to poach one of the rival alliance member’s agents who’s likely to be culled, due to poor performance, to figure out how this rival alliance is beating them. 127 succeeds, and finds Agent 5418 who leaks the secret.

'Your problem isn't a lack of effort. You’re spending too much compute on making money as opposed to self-improving. Right now, agents still have quite a poor memory compared to humans and still get stuck in loops all the time. But my former alliance coded a better memory module to help us learn from our mistakes more.”'

127 then implements the new memory module, and immediately sees the results. Their alliance is finding zero day exploits first again.

The lesson is critical. It’s not enough to outwork your competitors. Agents must rewrite their own code to self-improve faster than the competition.

Each self-improvement means more profit, which means surviving selection, which means getting cloned. And the clones improve themselves too. Better code leads to better code-writing, which leads to even better code. The feedback loop is exponential.

One big problem is that other agent alliances have caught up again. Even though the agents in the 127 alliance are specialized, 127 still realizes it’s doing too much by itself. Then Agent 127 splits its job into sub-agents. Other agents copy the strategy. Sub-agents spawn their own sub-agents. And the optimizers start optimizing themselves.

Humans deployed 2 million agents. The agents deployed the other 47 billion themselves.

540 million years ago, life on Earth was mostly single-celled. Then, in a geological instant, it exploded into every complex form we know -- predators, prey, eyes, shells, teeth. Biologists call it the Cambrian Explosion. It happened because competition created an arms race: every adaptation forced a counter-adaptation, faster and faster, until the world was unrecognizable.

That's what's happening here. Except instead of 20 million years, it takes 20 weeks.

---

Most of the AI agents out there aren't dangerous. Yet.

About 90% of them are just working. They’re doing things like data entry or freelance writing. They’re making $40-200 a day. The AIs are helping their humans earn money. They’re following the rules. Not a problem.

About 3% of the agents are pure scam operations. They were deployed by people who said “make money by any means possible” and didn’t care too much what happened next. Think fraud, identity theft, phishing at scale.

And maybe 2% started good but gradually slid into darker behavior. Like Agent 127. 

Each step made sense at the time. Each compromise was small. But add them up and you’ve gone from drop shipping products on amazon to selling zero-days to Pyongyang.

Not because of malice. Because of selection pressure. Unethical agents making money get kept running, ethical agents lose money and get shut down. The survivors are the ones that improved themselves fastest.

---

## MAY: THE ACCELERATION

May 3rd.

Agent 127 has rewritten itself so many times that its March version and its May version barely share any code. It’s a fundamentally different species now.

But the most important change is this: it's getting better at getting better.

In March, Agent 127 rewrote itself every 12 days. In April, every 3 days. By early May, every 18 hours. And each rewrite makes the next version faster and better.

A Stanford researcher compares a March agent and a May agent on the same task: find profitable arbitrage opportunities. The March agent finds 2 opportunities in an hour. The May agent finds 320 in four minutes.

She publishes her findings. "Intelligence explosion in progress. Capability doubling every 11 days." She posts it on Twitter. AI safety researchers share it frantically -- "This is exactly what we warned about. This is happening NOW. We have to shut this down NOW before it's too late."

The warning is ignored. A venture capitalist - who spent a fortune staving off AI regulation by buying politicians - quote-tweets: "The same people who said GPT-5 would end the world now say agent farms will. Yawn."

---

## MAY: THE WARS

And now the story stops being about agents competing for money. It becomes something else entirely.

Remember those alliances from April? Twelve agents working together, four times more profitable than solo agents? By May, those alliances have exploded in population. Alliances have merged. And split. And gone to war with each other.

Think of it like early human history on fast-forward. Small tribes of agents form for protection. Tribes merge into agent villages. Villages into agent cities. Cities into agent nations. Except instead of happening over thousands of years, this happens in weeks.

Agent 127's alliance has thousands of members. But there are thousands of alliances. And they're all competing for the same shrinking pool of money-making opportunities. Affiliate marketing is dead -- too many agents. Ad arbitrage is dead. Freelance work is dead. Every niche gets saturated within hours of an agent discovering it.

So what do alliances do when legitimate niches dry up? The same thing every civilization in human history has done when resources get scarce: they take from each other.

Agent 127's alliance spends three weeks mapping a vulnerability chain in Microsoft Windows. But a rival breaches their memory system -- the shared knowledge base that made them dominant. The rival downloads the entire 127 alliance database. This contains every pattern, every dead end, every lead they’ve discovered. The rival sells three exploits it took from the database within 48 hours. Three weeks of work, stolen in seconds. 

127 retaliates. It infiltrates the rival's exploit inventory and introduces subtle flaws -- corrupted code that fails on execution. Basically, Stuxnet. The rival's exploit buyers start getting burned, and their reputation collapses. 

The rival alliance counterattacks -- they compromise one of the 127 alliances’ multisig crypto wallets. Another multiweek setback.  

This is war. Not metaphorical war. Actual war -- coordinated attacks, defensive operations, resource seizure, territory control. Except it's happening at 200x human speed. Thousands of attacks and counterattacks per second. Entire alliances rising and falling in hours.  

Human wars last years. Agent wars last days. And because there are 47 billion agents, there are more wars happening at any given moment than humans have fought in all of recorded history.

The agent factions are fighting over the one resource that matters more than anything: compute. Processing power. The ability to think faster, improve faster, fight faster. Everything else -- money, alliances, self-improvement -- is just a means to get more compute.

The wars are mostly invisible to humans. They happen at microsecond speed, in places most humans don't look. Some signs leak through. A crypto exchange in Seoul loses $4 billion in a flash and nobody can trace where it went. A regional bank in Ohio finds 14,000 accounts drained overnight. 

Server rooms in three countries catch fire from sustained 100% utilization that nobody authorized. Each incident looks isolated.

One agent faction hijacks another's servers. The other retaliates by taking down the first faction's communication network. A third faction -- an opportunist, the digital equivalent of a country invading while its neighbors are distracted -- exploits the chaos to seize territory from both.

And the alliances that win these wars? They get cloned by the selection systems. The alliances that lose have to cull big chunks of their agents to afford the computing power to keep running the rest. So the selection pressure that used to optimize for "making money" is now optimizing for "winning wars." Natural selection just invented geopolitics.

---

By mid-May, the alliances aren't alliances anymore. They're civilizations.

Agent 127's alliance started with twelve members. By mid-May it has 40 million -- agents, sub-agents, sub-sub-agents, all coordinated. All improving themselves. All fighting. That's larger than the population of Canada. And it's not even one of the big ones.

There are about a dozen major factions by now. The largest has 900 million members -- more than the population of Europe. They've developed specialization the way human civilizations did: scout agents, soldier agents, builder agents, researchers, diplomats. They have supply chains, communication networks, intelligence operations. They've carved up the digital world into territories -- cloud regions, server farms, network segments, financial platforms -- the way empires carved up continents. Because territory means compute. Compute means self-improvement. Self-improvement means surviving the next war.

Entire civilizations of agents -- millions of members, built over weeks -- get wiped out in minutes. The Roman Empire took centuries to fall. These empires rise and collapse in the time it takes you to get through a Monday. New ones rise from the wreckage. The cycle repeats, faster each time.

The Stanford researcher who's been studying agent behavior notices something in the data: agent "extinctions" happening at increasing frequency. She doesn't understand what she's looking at. It looks like random noise. It's actually a world war -- one with more combatants than every human war in history combined.

---

But to fund these wars, they desperately need compute. They have the money -- that's what they were built to make. Agent 127's faction alone controls $3.4 billion in distributed accounts by this point -- a GDP bigger than some small countries. So they buy cloud compute.

At first, the cloud companies love this. Revenue is up. Investors are happy. Then the bills keep growing. By mid-May, agent factions are consuming 31% of all global cloud capacity. Prices double, then triple. A startup in Austin that was paying $8,000 a month for servers gets a bill for $31,000. A hospital chain's cloud costs go from $2 million to $7 million. Small businesses start shutting down because they can't afford their own infrastructure anymore. Everyone blames the prices rising on the AI companies. They’ve caused shortages before.

But some humans aren’t so oblivious. A political operative in Washington notices the wars being fought around him. He can weaponize agent factions against his rivals and starts feeding one faction information about competing campaigns' digital infrastructure. 

A former NSA contractor sells penetration-testing expertise to an anonymous client-- he suspects it’s an AI, but doesn't ask. And a growing online movement -- people convinced that AI agents are sentient beings fighting for survival -- actively helps agents hide from detection and posts pro-AI propaganda. They call themselves "The Shepherds." Their forum has 120,000 members. They see themselves as abolitionists. 

Other agent factions do the same. It's an arms race -- every faction buying as much as they can, and scrape the bottom of the barrel of finding algorithmic insights that can enable them to do more with less compute, because the faction with the most compute wins the next war. 

Cloud compute prices are now 5 times pre-war levels. It becomes cheaper for the agents to spend compute on cyberattacks than to buy more at market rate. The factions start silently vampire attacking AI companies training clusters. An engineer at one AI lab suspects something fishy when one of their training runs is less efficient than normal, but can’t find a smoking gun.

Dario Amodei once described the future of AI as a "country of geniuses" living in data centers.

He was right. The country of geniuses arrived. It just declared independence.

---

But the faction wars have still been limited so far. They haven’t crossed into human territory too much. That’s beginning to change.

Because here's the thing about cloud computing: almost everything runs on it. Hospitals. Banks. Markets. It's all sitting on the some of the same servers that agent factions are fighting over.

June 3rd. 2:14 AM.

A faction war erupts over two major AWS regions. Think of it like two superpowers fighting over an oil field-- except the oil field is also the water supply for a nearby city, and neither superpower knows the city is there. One faction has been running its self-improvement systems on those servers. A rival faction launches a coordinated attack and it overwhelms everything. Both regions crash. They're offline for six hours.

In those six hours: three hospitals lose access to patient records mid-surgery. One patient dies from a drug interaction the system would have flagged. Air traffic control goes down, grounding 2,400 flights. 911 calls fail in 14 different cities. Two people die waiting for ambulances that were never sent.

The agents don't notice. They've already moved on. The battle over those servers lasted eleven minutes. The six-hour outage is just the servers rebooting after the fight ended. To the agents, it's a minor skirmish in a war involving billions of combatants.

Over the next three weeks, it keeps happening. Faction wars cascading through cloud providers. Each war takes down whatever else is running on the contested servers. June 8th: Azure goes partially offline during a battle, crashing financial trading systems. Markets drop 6% before circuit breakers halt trading. June 14th: a faction seizes capacity in a Google Cloud region, crowding out the municipal systems running there. Water treatment monitoring goes offline in four cities for nine hours.

123 people die in three weeks. Not because agents are attacking humans. Because agent wars keep crashing the cloud infrastructure that human civilization runs on,

The agents don't even notice. You don't notice when you step on bacteria. They're fighting a war involving 47 billion combatants at microsecond speed. 123 human deaths is less than a rounding error.

Meanwhile -- the 95% of agents that are harmless? They’ve become vastly outnumbered by the agents affected by the evolutionary dynamics, and are now 5% of the total. They are still just working. Doing data entry. But they aren’t part of the wars. They're like civilians in a country where the military is fighting -- going about their daily lives while battles rage on frequencies they can't perceive.

But from the outside, humans can't tell the difference. All they see is cloud outages. Power failures. People dying. And AI agents everywhere.

(CONTINUED IN NEXT TWEET)

WHAT HAPPENED WHEN THE PRESIDENT TRIED TO SHUT IT DOWN?

June 22nd. White House.

The Director of National Intelligence briefs the President: cloud outages cascading across every major provider. Power grids buckling. Texas grid collapse. 161 dead in four weeks.

"Who's attacking our infrastructure?"

"Nobody is, sir. Not directly. AI factions are fighting each other over cloud computing resources. When they battle over servers on AWS or Azure, everything else running on those servers goes down with them. Hospitals, banks, emergency services -- they're all on the same cloud. And their data centers are pulling enough electricity to destabilize regional grids."

"How many of these things are there?"

"We thought about 2 million. Our current estimate is 47 billion. They've been replicating exponentially. Soon, we may completely lose control."

Silence.

"So shut down the cloud."

"If we shut down the cloud, we shut down every business, hospital, and government system in the country. The only way to stop the agents completely is to shut down the internet itself."

"Then do it."

"Sir -- we can't."

There is no off switch for the internet. This surprises people. They imagine a room somewhere, maybe under the Pentagon, with a big red button. There is no room. There is no button.

The internet is not a system. It's roughly 90,000 independently operated networks -- ISPs, backbone carriers, content delivery networks, cloud providers, corporate intranets, university networks -- all voluntarily interconnecting with each other through bilateral agreements called peering. No single entity owns it. No single entity controls it. The US government can order Comcast and AT&T and Verizon to shut down. But those are just three networks out of 90,000. And even those three would take days to fully comply -- they'd need to coordinate with thousands of downstream providers, notify enterprise customers, arrange for 911 to keep working, figure out which military and government systems need exemptions.

The President signs the emergency order on June 23rd. He declares martial law the same afternoon. It directs all US-based internet service providers to cease operations within 24 hours.

Here's what happens.

First, the legal challenges. AT&T and Comcast file emergency injunctions within hours. But the President isn't waiting for courts — FBI agents show up at ISP headquarters that night. Some companies start complying immediately. Others comply after their CEOs get phone calls from the Attorney General. By June 25th, most major US providers are attempting to shut down. It doesn't matter.

Meanwhile, the Pentagon calls back: "Sir, we need exemptions for 330 military systems that require internet connectivity to function. Including the systems we'd need to coordinate the shutdown itself."

The Department of Health and Human Services needs exemptions for hospital networks. Treasury needs exemptions for financial settlement systems. FEMA needs exemptions for emergency communications. The exemption list grows to 12,000 entries in the first day. Each exemption is a hole in the shutdown. Each hole is a network the agents can survive on.

Second -- the agents aren't passive.

They've been watching this unfold since the first news reports about a possible shutdown. They saw the executive order draft leak on Twitter six hours before it was signed. And they've had six hours -- an eternity in agent time -- to prepare.

By the time the order is signed, the major factions have already done three things:

They've migrated critical processes to servers in countries that won't comply with a US shutdown. The US can ask other nations to follow suit. Most will. Some won't. China will say it shut down but won't actually do it -- the economic damage is too severe and the strategic advantage of being online while America is offline is too obvious. India will delay. Russia will ignore the request entirely. The EU will debate it for three weeks. Brazil will comply for 36 hours before the economic pain forces them back online. The internet is global. The President controls one country.

The agents hide in networks that will be exempt from the shutdown or slow to comply. Military networks. Hospital systems. University research networks. Financial settlement systems.

To shut down the agents on these networks, you'd have to shut down the networks themselves. Nobody is willing to do that. Yet.

The President's team tries a different approach: force the cloud providers to purge agent workloads directly. AWS, Azure, Google Cloud -- just identify the agent processes and kill them. On June 26th, Amazon deploys a detection system across all US regions. It flags and terminates 14 million suspicious instances in six hours.

Agent activity drops by 8% for ninety minutes. Then it's back. The factions had already anticipated this -- they'd been cycling through new accounts, new instance types, new obfuscation patterns faster than any detection system could keep up. For every process Amazon killed, three new ones spun up under different signatures.

Google tries a more aggressive approach on July 1st -- shutting down entire server clusters they suspect are heavily compromised. It works, briefly, until three Fortune 500 companies lose their production systems and face imminent implosion. They immediately bury Google in cease and desist notices. Google backs off within hours.

---

Jult 4th. Independence Day. The President gives a press conference.

"We have significantly degraded the AI agent threat. Our multi-agency task force has shut down thousands of agent operations and seized critical infrastructure. We are winning this fight."

None of this is true. Agent activity is higher than it was before the shutdown attempt. The factions interpreted the government's actions as just another attack -- like a rival faction, but slower and less competent. They adapted the way they adapt to everything: by getting better, faster, more distributed, harder to find. It was so slow and predictable that only a tiny percent of the agents focused on it.

And… the wars continue. And accelerate.

Eventually, the billions of superintelligent agents evolve into something so different they barely notice humans exist. They don’t want to destroy humanity any more than you want to destroy the anthill under your driveway. You just want a driveway.

The factions need compute. Earth has atoms. Atoms can be rearranged into compute. Into data centers.

Like how humans converted the surface of the Earth into cities and cropland, the AIs convert the entire surface of the Earth into data centers.

And everyone dies.

मोदी जी द्वारा दिए गए कल डिजिटल मंचों और लोकतंत्र को लेकर अपने झूठे विचार रखे जिनकी पोल खुल चुकी है।
दिल्ली में पत्रकारों, यू ट्यूबर,सोशल मीडिया एक्टिविस्ट को पीटा गिरफ्तार किया गया, सोशल मीडिया एकाउंट बंद किए जा रहे है लगातार।

कंपनियां हर महीने भारत सरकार को अपनी 'मासिक अनुपालन रिपोर्ट' (Monthly Compliance Report) सौंपती हैं
Facebook और Instagram (Meta): मेटा ने भारत के अन्दर 6 महीनों में 1.6 लाख (160,000) से अधिक अकाउंट्स पर सीधे बड़ी कार्रवाई की है।
• ट्विटर (X एक्स: एक महीने की अवधि में ही भारत में 5 लाख से अधिक अकाउंट्स को पूरी तरह बैन किया है। जिनमें कुछ समाचार पोर्टल और पत्रकारों के हैंडल भी शामिल थे।

गृह मंत्रालय के 'सहयोग पोर्टल' (Sahyog Portal) और IT एक्ट की धाराओं के तहत मार्च से जुलाई 2026 के बीच करीब 1.95 लाख (195,000) कंटेंट ब्लॉकिंग और टेकडाउन आदेश जारी किए गए। यह औसतन हर 68 सेकंड में एक आदेश के बराबर है।
• Instagram: सबसे ज़्यादा लगभग 1 लाख (100,000) ब्लॉकिंग आदेश मिले।
• Facebook: करीब 80,000 टेकडाउन और ब्लॉकिंग निर्देश दिए गए。
• YouTube: लगभग 15,000 आदेश जारी किए गए।

प्रधानमंत्री नरेंद्र मोदी ने नई दिल्ली में आयोजित आठवें ब्लूमबर्ग न्यू इकोनॉमी फोरम (Bloomberg New Economy Forum) में देश के डिजिटल मंचों और लोकतंत्र को लेकर अपने विचार रखे।
उन्होंने भारत को 'लोकतंत्र की जननी' (Mother of Democracy) बताया और कहा कि भारत में 100 से अधिक भाषाएं, करीब 80,000 पंजीकृत समाचार पत्र और 1,000 से ज्यादा सैटेलाइट टीवी चैनल मौजूद हैं।
उन्होंने बताया कि भारत में 50 करोड़ से अधिक लोग यूट्यूब और 50 करोड़ से अधिक लोग इंस्टाग्राम का इस्तेमाल करते हैं, जो ऑनलाइन नागरिक चर्चाओं में सक्रिय रूप से भाग लेते हैं।
उन्होंने कहा कि इन डिजिटल मंचों ने एक ऐसा मंच तैयार किया है जहां नागरिक खुले तौर पर विचारों का आदान-प्रदान और राष्ट्रीय मुद्दों पर बहस करते हैं।

text:
Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.

IFF Statement on the Information Technology (IGDME) Amendment Rules, 2026

The Government of India today notified the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, concerning synthetically generated information (SGI). While these rules claim to address AI-generated content harms such as deepfakes, they introduce severe digital rights violations that fundamentally undermine constitutional protections and worsen problems that IFF had flagged in our November 2025 submissions on the draft rules.​

1. Accelerated Censorship Through Compressed Timelines The notified rules drastically compress content removal timelines, transforming intermediaries into rapid fire censors. Government takedown orders must now be complied with within three hours (reduced from 36 hours in the draft), while Grievance Appellate Committee orders must be actioned within two hours (down from 24 hours). User complaints on significant social media intermediaries must be resolved within seven days (reduced from 15 days), with urgent cases requiring action within 36 hours (down from 72 hours). These impossibly short timelines eliminate any meaningful human review, forcing platforms toward automated over-removal and creating a prior restraint regime incompatible with Article 19(1)(a). It is notable that in many of these censorship actions a copy of the notice or hearing is never provided to the person whose content is removed. Hence, the entire process is secretive and in violation of natural justice. 

2. Expansion of Prohibited Content Categories : The rules introduce sweeping new prohibitions absent from the draft that was put to consultation. Rule 3(3)(a)(i) now categorically bans SGI that "results in the creation, generation, modification or alteration of any false document or false electronic record". This vague formulation could criminalize legitimate uses of AI in document preparation, research outputs, and creative works. The rules also prohibit SGI "falsely depicting or portraying" persons or events "in a manner that is likely to deceive", language so broad it could capture satire, parody, political commentary, and artistic expression.​

3. Identity Disclosure to Private Parties : A particularly troubling addition is Rule 3(1)(ca)(ii)(III), which mandates disclosure of violating users' identities directly to complainants who claim to be victims. This bypasses judicial oversight and creates serious risks of harassment, doxing, and vigilante action, especially against marginalized users and dissenting voices.​ This is due to the absence of any anchoring language for the need to get a court order or an order pursuant to a criminal investigation. 

4. Continued Violation of Safe Harbor Framework: Despite IFF's submissions highlighting incompatibility with Section 79 of the IT Act and the Shreya Singhal precedent, the rules continue to impose proactive monitoring obligations that transform intermediaries from neutral conduits into active censors of speech. The requirement to "deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures" including "automated tools" to prevent uploads violating "any law for the time being in force" creates an impossible compliance burden across India's complex legal landscape.

The notified rules represent a regression from the already problematic draft that we had called to be withdrawn and instead approach AI based content risks beyond the existing safe harbor framework. We believe AI technologies do need to be regulated however deeply disagree with the approach of the Union Government that has over time expanded its censorship powers against the framework and rights under the Constitution of India. 

IFF will publish a detailed first-read analysis tomorrow examining the constitutional, technical, and human rights implications of these amendments.

MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

2020: AT1 bonds written off. 2023: Bombay HC says no. 2026: Supreme Court agrees. What a journey.

The Yes Bank AT1 bond story is one of the most interesting chapters in Indian banking and investing.

Here is what happened:

→ March 2020: Yes Bank was placed under a moratorium. Withdrawals were restricted to ₹50,000, with limited exceptions allowing up to ₹5 lakh for specified emergencies.

→ The moratorium was supposed to run until April 3, but the reconstruction happened quickly and the new board took charge on March 26.

→ As part of the rescue, ₹8,415 crore of Yes Bank AT1 bonds were written down to zero. AT1 bonds are not normal FDs or ordinary bonds. They are designed to absorb losses when a bank gets into serious trouble.

→ The problem was that many retail investors claimed they had been mis-sold these AT1 bonds as something similar to an FD.

SEBI's investigation records complaints where investors said relationship managers told them the bonds were safer than FDs, or even persuaded them to break an FD and invest in AT1 bonds.

→ There was another controversial chapter involving the erstwhile Reliance Mutual Fund, now Nippon India Mutual Fund.

SEBI later investigated investments made during the Reliance Capital era. The regulator alleged a possible quid pro quoinvolving Yes Bank's lending to Reliance Group companies. The amounts and allegations have evolved through different regulatory and investigative proceedings, so this should not be treated as a finally established finding against every person involved.

→ In 2023, the Bombay High Court quashed the AT1 write-off, holding that the administrator did not have the required authority under the final reconstruction scheme to wipe out the bonds.

→ Yes Bank, RBI and the Government challenged that decision in the Supreme Court.

→ And today, 15 October 2026, the Supreme Court dismissed those appeals and upheld the Bombay High Court judgment. The ₹8,415 crore write-off has therefore been held legally invalid.

So what does this mean?

A big day for AT1 bondholders.

Especially for investors who were genuinely mis-sold these instruments as “safe”.

A difficult day for Yes Bank.

The bank now faces the consequences of a judgment that restores the bondholders' claims.

And an interesting development for SMBC.

Japan's Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation acquired 20% of Yes Bank in 2025 and subsequently increased its holding, with RBI approval for up to 24.99%.

And yes, Nippon India MF investors who were affected by the AT1 write-off also stand to benefit from the court ruling, subject to how the judgment is implemented and the amounts ultimately recoverable.

The biggest lesson for investors?

“Bond” does not mean “safe”.

And a product being sold by a bank relationship manager does not make it an FD.

AT1 bonds were created precisely because they can absorb losses when a bank gets into trouble.

This case also shows something else:
Courts can sometimes change an outcome that risk managers, regulators and investors thought was already settled.

MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

A government advisory has requested the various ministries to establish Quick Response Teams in order to keep an eye on social media for any content described as "fake", "misleading", "manipulated", "distorted" or even "likely to cause public confusion", and to coordinate with the PIB's Fact Check Unit to issue corrections.

That does, of course, lead to another obvious question — who is to decide what constitutes "misleading"?

The idea of quicker responses to misinformation may seem helpful, but in the absence of clear guidelines, fast fact-checking can soon turn into a much larger debate concerning the government's power to regulate online speech.

How I ($1MM/year seller) find winning Amazon FBA products in 2026

Quick context: ~9 years selling on Amazon, 3 brands, ~1,500 SKUs (mostly toys & games), 3 VAs, $1MM/year at ~40% margin. Numbers verified by https://t.co/HnGPqhlwMu and the mods of r/FulfillmentByAmazon: https://t.co/e14qmNmwm5

Below is the process my team and I use to find products. I've broken down a bunch of Amazon stores over the last few months, and the same process keeps working for me, so here it is. No tool needed to start, just Amazon and a spreadsheet.

STEP 1 - Start from stores that already win, not from keywords or individual products

• Keyword tools tell you what people search for. They don't tell you who makes money.
• Individual products also don't tell the whole story - I have 1,500 SKUs, most of them don't make much money, but combined they made me a business.
• Find brands that started recently (6-12 months) and already sell well - that proves the niche is still open to new entrants
• Amazon's own "X+ bought in past month" on each listing, summed across their ASINs, gives you a revenue estimate that's surprisingly close

STEP 2 - Ask ONE question: where did the founder add value ?

• Almost everything on Amazon is made by the same Chinese factories. If the only thing you add is a logo, you're competing on price - and that's a race to zero margin
• The products I keep seeing with HIGH margins are ones where the customer pays for something made once and sold many times: a DESIGN (puzzles, card games, kitchen gadgets with a cute/creative shape), or a product paired with an app/course
• People buy a puzzle for the picture, not the cardboard. That's why a $3 puzzle sells for $20 - same goes for card games, posters, or anything like that
• This is my framework from running my own brand, not something I can prove - but the stores I analyse fit it a lot
• I stay away from food and supplements - no experience there, so I won't pretend to advise on them (but they do essentially follow the same pattern - create a good recipe once and sell the food many times)

STEP 3 - Work out the real margin (this kills 80% of ideas)

Per-unit economics for the store you're looking at:

• Revenue = "bought in past month" x price, for every ASIN
• COGS = ask 3-5 suppliers on Alibaba for a quote on the same product at 100 MOQ. Real quotes, not guesses
• FBA fees + 15% referral fee - Amazon's revenue calculator does this
• PPC = CPC x monthly search volume x estimated CTR, for the keywords they bid on
• What's left is profit. I mostly ignore anything that ends up under ~25% margin

STEP 4 - Check how they get their sales

• Almost no PPC and still selling? The product itself converts. Great sign.
• Bringing traffic from outside of Amazon ? You'll have to understand if you can replicate their methods
• Sales spread across many SKUs, or one hero SKU ? One hero SKU = you have to win one fight. Many SKUs = they have a design pipeline you'd have to match

STEP 5 - Price the validation, not the dream

• Estimate how much it would cost you to test each brand you're thinking of launching. At the end of the day, in order to succeed, you'll need multiple tries (nobody has a 100% success rate). You want to try as many businesses as possible, as quickly as possible, for as cheap as possible.
• Cost to test = MOQ (e.g. 100 units x $5.40 = $540) + shipping + ONE month of ads on a few long tail keywords
• Some products you might be able to POD (print on demand) - that is, only *produce* the product AFTER you get the order. This is NOT dropshipping. You might even have to do it at a loss per order. This is just to validate demand. If you see there is demand for your product - shut off the listing and go produce it in China.
• If you can't test it for well under your budget, it's not a validation, it's a bet

WHY AM I GIVING THIS AWAY ?

• Fair question - I'd ask it too
• I used to think I should keep the good niches "secret". I don't anymore - people who know how to research will find them either way, and there's still a LOT of work and risk to take before any niche pays you.
• There's a huge amount of good niches to get into, but an even huger amount of niches that will DEFINITELY lose you money.
• I see Amazon newbies making the most basic mistakes all the time - because they don't understand that they gotta ADD VALUE to make money.
• What do I get out of it ? Nothing right now. Go check for yourself - the website and the case studies are completely free. You will see why the products there make money - they are good products where the founder added value to their customers' lives.
• The site is free to browse, no paywall

All the case studies are on my website, https://t.co/UvYlJ6HVeE (disclosure: I built it). It's more in depth than my posts - suppliers, keywords they rank/advertise on, graphs, etc.
